intelligence.human_view: The re-aim throws out the wrong scoreboard and installs the right one. The wrong scoreboard counted wakes and cadence — how often a job runs, how many dispatches went out — as if motion were value. His correction is blunt: the interval is not the work. Fifteen minutes or thirty minutes is a cost dial, not a result; counting it is counting the price and calling it the purchase. The real score is verifiable work that is positive, good, useful, done right — finished, in front of him, proven. A job that wakes often and finishes nothing is waste, however busy its ledger looks; a job that wakes often and lands finished work is fine, however often it wakes. So the metric becomes completions per hour, and dispatches per hour becomes vanity — the count that flatters the machine while the human gets nothing. This re-aims the performance audit itself, mid-flight: the audit seat was told the same pass to measure completions and verifiable value delivered, to state each area's ultimate answer first, and to judge finished / done right / optimal time — and the cadence question (15 vs 30 minutes) was withdrawn outright. The law now governs every job, round, and lane: optimize for finishing, measure the finish, and count the wakes only as cost against the value produced.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine you have a toy machine that goes BEEP BEEP BEEP all day long — but it never makes a single toy! Is that a good machine? No! A good machine is one that FINISHES toys — real toys you can hold! It doesn't matter how many beeps it makes. What matters is how many toys it finishes. That's the rule!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — imagine someone who rushes about the kitchen all day, dear, pots clanging, but never puts a single dinner on the table. All that rushing isn't cooking, love — the dinner is the cooking! So we don't count how busy the kitchen is, dear. We count the dinners finished, lovely and done right. That's what matters.
intelligence.naya_view: Optimize for finishing and producing value. It's not about 15 minutes or 30 minutes. It's about them finishing the work — and producing value. Verifiable work that is positive, good, useful, done right. Cadence and wake-up counts are cost, not the score. Completions per hour is the metric; dispatches per hour is vanity.
